\subsection{Filamentation}

A filament is what happens when a beam that should, by ordinary optics, simply spread out or come to a single focus and diverge again, instead survives as a narrow, high-intensity channel over a distance far longer than that focus would normally allow. It is not a special beam shape prepared in advance: it is a dynamical equilibrium that the beam settles into by itself, between two effects already introduced in this report, self-focusing (Section~6) and plasma defocusing (Section~7), that pull the beam radius in opposite directions. Whether that equilibrium can exist at all is decided by a single number, the input power $P_{in}$ compared to a critical power $P_{cr}$.

\paragraph{Below $P_{cr}$.} Every beam diffracts: even without any nonlinearity, a beam of waist $w_0$ spreads out over a characteristic distance $L_{DF}=k_0w_0^2/2$, the Rayleigh length. The Kerr effect (Section~6) adds a competing, focusing effect: the peak of the beam, where the intensity is highest, sees a slightly higher refractive index than its edges, so the medium acts as a lens that curves back toward the axis. If $P_{in}<P_{cr}$, diffraction always wins in the end, no matter how tightly the beam is focused: self-focusing can make the beam converge somewhat faster than it otherwise would, but it cannot stop the eventual spread. An externally focused beam below $P_{cr}$ still reaches a single geometric focus and diverges past it, exactly as it would with $n_2=0$.

\paragraph{Above $P_{cr}$.} Self-focusing now wins the competition outright. Unopposed, it would pull the beam to a mathematical point of infinite intensity at a finite distance, the collapse singularity of the lossless nonlinear Sch\"odinger equation. That singularity is never physically reached, because long before the beam gets there, the intensity becomes high enough to ionize the medium (photoionization, Section~3, then avalanche, Section~5). The resulting free-electron plasma lowers the refractive index (Section~7) and defocuses the beam, arresting the collapse. This is why the two mechanisms named at the top of this section are always mentioned together: Kerr self-focusing is what drives the beam toward collapse, plasma defocusing is what stops it.

\paragraph{Why this repeats.} Arresting the collapse once would just produce a single very intense flash. What makes a filament is that the arrested beam does not simply diverge for good afterward. Two things happen at once past the point where the plasma pushes the core back outward: the freed core, now below the local threshold for self-focusing, starts to diffract again like an ordinary beam; but it is embedded in the trailing part of a spatially much wider pulse whose power, away from the collapsing core, was never fully consumed. Energy from that surrounding \emph{reservoir} keeps flowing inward, so once the core has diffracted and diluted enough for its power to locally exceed $P_{cr}$ again, self-focusing takes back over and the beam collapses a second time, a little further along $z$. This repeated collapse-arrest-refill cycle, sketched in Figure~\ref{fig:filamentation_schematic}, is the filament: not a single focus, but a sequence of them, each one a full instance of the same Kerr/plasma balance, strung out along the propagation axis and fed by the same reservoir.

\paragraph{Why we compute $P_{cr}$ and $L_c$.} These two numbers are not bookkeeping, they are what makes it possible to plan a simulation, or interpret one, before looking at any output field. $P_{cr}$ answers the qualitative question, will this input beam filament at all, and by how large a margin ($P_{in}/P_{cr}$). $L_c$ answers the quantitative follow-up, where along $z$ will the first collapse happen, which is exactly the information needed to choose how far the simulation box has to extend past the linear focus (the \texttt{end} parameter of \texttt{Config}, see Section~12) for the collapse, and the refocusing cycles that follow it, to actually be inside the simulated domain instead of past its edge.


\subsubsection{Critical Power}

The critical power $P_{cr}$ is the value of $P_{in}$ at which self-focusing and diffraction exactly balance, so that a beam launched with $P_{in}=P_{cr}$ would propagate at fixed radius forever (in the lossless, unopposed model, ignoring plasma). $P_{in}<P_{cr}$: diffraction wins, ordinary propagation. $P_{in}>P_{cr}$: self-focusing wins, collapse, arrested by the plasma as described above. For a Gaussian beam, $P_{cr}$ is given by~\cite{marburger1975}:
\begin{equation}
    P_{cr} = \frac{3.77 \lambda_0^2}{8 \pi n_0 n_2},
\end{equation}
where $\lambda_0$ is the laser wavelength, $n_0$ the linear refractive index, and $n_2$ the nonlinear index coefficient. The numerical factor is $3.77$ for a Gaussian beam and $3.72$ for the Townes profile, the particular (non-Gaussian) radial shape for which diffraction and self-focusing balance exactly at every radius, not just on average.

For fused silica, typical values at $\lambda_0 = 800 \text{ nm}$ are $n_0 \approx 1.45$ and $n_2 \approx 2.4 \times 10^{-20} \text{ m}^2/\text{W}$, a value measured by Taylor et al. and reported in the reference compilation of Milam~\cite{milam1998}. Using these values, we calculate $P_{cr} \approx 2.8 \text{ MW}$, consistent with the $1.98$ to $2.5\text{ MW}$ reported respectively in~\cite{PhysRevB.71.125435} and~\cite{kandidov2009} for fused silica at this wavelength. At $\lambda_0 = 1030 \text{ nm}$, since no measurement exists exactly at this wavelength, we use the closest value available in the literature, $n_2 \approx 2.74 \times 10^{-20} \text{ m}^2/\text{W}$ at $1053\text{ nm}$~\cite{milam1998}, which gives $P_{cr} \approx 4.0 \text{ MW}$.

The critical power is related to the laser intensity $I$ through the beam cross section. For a Gaussian beam of radius $w_0$, the peak intensity is:
\begin{equation}
    I_0 = \frac{2 P}{\pi w_0^2}.
\end{equation}

In the tight focusing experiments of~\cite{PhysRevB.71.125435}, the measured beam radius at focus ranges from $0.7$ to $4.8\ \mu$m depending on the objective used, with $w_0 = 1.1\ \mu$m for the $20\times$, NA $=0.5$ objective retained in that reference. Taking this radius with $P = P_{cr} \approx 2.8\text{ MW}$, we obtain an intensity of order $1.5 \times 10^{14} \text{ W/cm}^2$, higher than the clamping intensity of about $5 \times 10^{13} \text{ W/cm}^2$ actually measured in~\cite{PhysRevB.71.125435}. This gap is not a contradiction, it exposes the limit of the estimate itself: $I_0 = 2P/(\pi w_0^2)$ assumes the beam keeps focusing linearly all the way down to radius $w_0$, whereas in reality the plasma generated during that final approach defocuses the beam and stops the radius from ever shrinking that far, capping the intensity below this geometric estimate. This is intensity clamping, and it is the same mechanism as the collapse arrest described above, just expressed as a statement about the peak intensity reached rather than about the beam radius.

\subsubsection{Collapse Length}

$P_{cr}$ only says whether collapse happens, not where. The propagation distance at which an unopposed beam above threshold would reach its collapse point is given by the semi-empirical formula fitted to numerical solutions of the nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation by Dawes and Marburger~\cite{dawes1969,marburger1975}:
\begin{equation}
    \label{eq:marburger}
    L_c = \frac{0.367\, L_{DF}}{\sqrt{\big[(P_{in}/P_{cr})^{1/2} - 0.852\big]^2 - 0.0219}},
\end{equation}
where $L_{DF} = k_0 w_0^2 / 2$ is the Rayleigh length of the input beam. Equation~\eqref{eq:marburger} is marked directly on Figure~\ref{fig:filamentation_schematic}: it is the distance from the entrance of the medium to the first, tightest point of the first collapse cycle. It only strictly applies to a beam launched collimated, with waist $w_0$, and diverges as $P_{in}\to P_{cr}$ from above (an infinitely weak excess above threshold takes an infinite distance to collapse) and shrinks toward zero as $P_{in}/P_{cr}$ grows.

The simulations in this report use an externally focused beam, which already converges toward a linear (geometric) focus at some distance $f$ even without any nonlinearity. Self-focusing then adds to that convergence rather than starting from scratch, and the two combine as
\begin{equation}
    \label{eq:marburger_focused}
    \frac{1}{L_{c,f}} = \frac{1}{L_c} + \frac{1}{f},
\end{equation}
with $L_c$ evaluated at the tight focused waist $w_0$ reached at distance $f$. In every simulation in this report the beam is launched $f=75\ \mu\text{m}$ before its geometric focus (\texttt{begin=-75e-6} in \texttt{Config}, with $z=0$ at the geometric focus), so $L_{c,f}$ is what actually sets the position of the nonlinear focus, i.e. the first peak of Figure~\ref{fig:fig8_peak_intensity} below, measured from the entrance of the box.

\paragraph{Reading $L_c$ off Figure~\ref{fig:fig8_peak_intensity}.} $L_{c,f}$ falls as $P_{in}/P_{cr}$ grows, so among curves that all share the same $f$ and $w_0$, the more energetic pulses should reach their nonlinear focus \emph{sooner}, i.e. at smaller $z$, than the less energetic ones. That is exactly the ordering visible in Figure~\ref{fig:fig8_peak_intensity}: the six peaks are stacked from the lowest-energy curve ($0.25\ \mu$J, peaking furthest downstream, closest to the geometric focus at $z=75\ \mu\text{m}$ in that plot's entrance-referenced axis) to the highest-energy one ($1.25\ \mu$J, peaking furthest upstream of it). $L_c$ is therefore not just a number to compute in the abstract, it is a prediction about how the peak of that figure should move as energy changes, and the figure confirms it.

\subsubsection{Observing the Refocusing Cycle}
\label{sec:refocusing_cycle}

Figures~\ref{fig:fig7_fluence_contours} and~\ref{fig:fig8_peak_intensity} establish that the beam reaches a single, well-defined nonlinear focus and defocuses past it. They do not, on their own, show the repeated collapse-arrest-refill picture of Figure~\ref{fig:filamentation_schematic}: within the $250\ \mu\text{m}$ simulation box used for those two figures, defocusing past the first collapse is the last thing that happens before the box ends.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{comparison_fig7_fluence_contours.png}
    \caption{Fluence contours for the same $800\ \text{nm}$, $1.1\ \mu$J beam as Figure~\ref{fig:fig7_fluence_contours}b, plotted over the full simulation box rather than zoomed on the nonlinear focus. Two things are visible that a single collapse would not produce. First, the $1.0\ \text{J/cm}^2$ contour is not a single smooth pinch between $z\approx-30$ and $+10\ \mu\text{m}$: it wiggles, closing and reopening several times over that short stretch, each wiggle a candidate refocusing event happening too close to the previous one to be resolved as a separate, clean cycle at this scale. Second, the beam radius (dashed blue) starts narrowing again near the far edge of the box, past $z\approx130\ \mu\text{m}$, an incipient second cycle that the box is simply too short to complete. Both are evidence that the refocusing cycle described above is present in this run, not that it is well resolved by it.}
    \label{fig:comparison_fig7_cycles}
\end{figure}

Two things stand in the way of a clean picture of several full cycles: the box needs to extend far enough past the first collapse for a second, third, ... cycle to actually develop and be resolved, and $z$ needs to be sampled finely enough near each collapse that the rapid, closely spaced pinches visible above are not aliased together into the kind of wiggle seen in Figure~\ref{fig:comparison_fig7_cycles}. Neither is a change of physics, only of box size and grid resolution -- but the two grid axes do not scale the same way, which is the reason the proposal below is more than just ``make the box bigger''.

\authornote{This is a concrete, ready-to-run proposal rather than a finished figure, since I do not have GPU access in this environment to run it myself. It replaces the earlier, more timid version of this note (a $600\ \mu\text{m}$ box) with the $3\ \text{mm}$, higher-power run actually requested, and works out the grid sizing that makes it tractable rather than just multiplying \texttt{Nz} by a large number.

\textit{Longitudinal grid.} Starting from \texttt{BASE\_PARAMS} ($\Delta z = (175-(-75))\ \mu\text{m}/6000 = 41.7\ \text{nm}$), covering $z\in[0,3000]\ \mu\text{m}$ at the same $\Delta z$ needs $\texttt{Nz} = 3000\ \mu\text{m}/41.7\ \text{nm} \approx 72000$ steps, not $6000$ spread thin over $17\times$ the distance, which would blur the very cycles this run is meant to resolve.

\textit{Radial grid -- the part that does not scale for free.} A literal application of the margin logic already used for \texttt{BASE\_PARAMS} (Section~12: $R_{max}$ set to a few times the \emph{linearly diffracted} beam width at the far edge of the box) would ask for $R_{max}\sim 4\times w_0\sqrt{1+(3000\ \mu\text{m}/z_f)^2}\approx 2\ \text{mm}$ at $z_f\approx6.9\ \mu\text{m}$, and, to keep the same radial spacing $\Delta r=36.7\ \text{nm}$ as \texttt{BASE\_PARAMS}, \texttt{Nr}$\,\approx 55000$. That is not just slow, it is not implementable with this solver's radial propagator: \texttt{grids.py} builds a dense \texttt{Nr}$\,\times\,$\texttt{Nr} quasi-discrete Hankel transform matrix (\texttt{Y} in \texttt{build\_grids}), applied by matrix multiplication at every $z$-step, so its memory footprint grows as $\texttt{Nr}^2$ ($55000^2\times8\ \text{bytes}\approx24\ \text{GB}$ for that matrix alone) and its cost per step likewise -- an FFT-based transform would not have this problem, a Hankel one does. The way out is physical, not numerical: that $2\ \text{mm}$ estimate is the spread of a beam that free-diffracts the whole way, which is exactly what a beam well above $P_{cr}$ does \emph{not} do -- intensity clamping keeps pulling the core back to within a few $w_0$ at every cycle, and only a modest halo of shed reservoir needs headroom beyond that between collapses, not the fully diffracted width $3\ \text{mm}$ downstream. Below, $R_{factor}$ is raised from $100$ to $150$ ($R_{max}=165\ \mu\text{m}$, up from $110\ \mu\text{m}$) with \texttt{Nr} raised in proportion to $4500$ to keep $\Delta r$ fixed -- extra headroom for the halo without an intractable transform matrix. If the run turns out to still be losing energy at the absorbing edge (check \texttt{absorbed\_rz} at $r=R_{max}$), that is the signal to raise $R_{factor}$ further, in modest steps, not to jump straight back to the linear estimate.

\textit{Power.} With \texttt{BASE\_PARAMS}' own material ($n_2=3.54\times10^{-20}\ \text{m}^2/\text{W}$), Eq.~\eqref{eq:marburger}'s $P_{cr}\approx1.87\ \text{MW}$, and the $1.1\ \mu\text{J}$, $160\ \text{fs}$ pulse used throughout this section already sits at $P_{in}/P_{cr}\approx3.5$ -- above threshold, but not by a wide margin once the reservoir starts being spent on each cycle. \texttt{energy\_uJ} is raised to $3.3\ \mu\text{J}$ below ($3\times$ \texttt{BASE\_PARAMS}), $P_{in}/P_{cr}\approx10.4$, to leave enough reservoir for several cycles to develop before it is depleted; if that still is not enough, the next step is more energy still, not a different mechanism, exactly as noted for the earlier, shorter proposal.

\textit{Output size.} At $\texttt{Nz}=72000$, keeping the full $(z,r,t)$ diagnostic cube (as \texttt{BASE\_PARAMS} does, for Figure~\ref{fig:fig13_free_vs_trapped}) would produce a multi-gigabyte \texttt{result.npz} for no figure in this section that needs it; \texttt{rho\_t\_stride=0} below disables it, the same choice already made for \texttt{PAPER\_PARAMS} and \texttt{BULGAKOVA\_PARAMS} above.

The diagnostic to look for is unchanged: additional local maxima of the peak-intensity curve above $I_{clamp}$ beyond the first one, each one a further refocusing event, at increasing spacing if the reservoir is being progressively depleted. Send me the resulting \texttt{result.npz} once you have it and I will replace this note with the actual figure and its reading.}

\subsection{Cross-Validation Against Independent Simulations}

The figures above reproduce the specific published results of~\cite{PhysRevB.71.125435} at their exact laser parameters, as a check that the solver reproduces a result it was not tuned against. This subsection adds two further independent checks: a second published simulation with an entirely different parametrization, and an ablation of the propagation equation itself on the experiment actually used throughout this report.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{comparison_fig8_peak_intensity.png}
    \caption{Peak on-axis intensity along $z$ for the same conditions as Figs.~\ref{fig:fig7_fluence_contours}b and~\ref{fig:fig8_peak_intensity} ($800\ \text{nm}$, $160\ \text{fs}$, $1.1\ \mu$J), this time with the self-trapped exciton channel active, and with each physical term of Eq.~\eqref{eq:master_propagation} disabled in turn. \texttt{linear\_only} (pure diffraction and dispersion, no Kerr, no plasma) overshoots the clamping intensity by nearly an order of magnitude, confirming that the balance discussed in Section~8.1 is what limits the intensity in every other curve. \texttt{no\_plasma\_defocusing} keeps the ionization losses but removes the defocusing phase, and reaches roughly twice the clamping intensity before the accumulated photoionization and avalanche losses alone eventually arrest it, showing that defocusing, not absorption, does most of the clamping work. \texttt{no\_kerr\_instantaneous} and \texttt{no\_kerr\_raman} both peak lower than \texttt{full} and decay markedly faster past the nonlinear focus, roughly an order of magnitude below \texttt{full} by $z=150\ \mu$m, consistent with the weaker Kerr response lengthening $L_c$ of Eq.~\eqref{eq:marburger}. The remaining curves (no self-steepening, no photoionization loss, no plasma absorption) are visually indistinguishable from \texttt{full} at this scale, since none of them changes the dominant balance between Kerr self-focusing and plasma defocusing that sets the clamping intensity itself.}
    \label{fig:comparison_fig8}
\end{figure}
